meta.title: Colorado developer funding resources
meta.scope: Programs that finance affordable rental and for-sale housing development in Colorado: federal and state tax credits, CHFA loans, Proposition 123 funds, Division of Housing funds, federal and agency debt and grants, rental assistance, and the largest city funds.
meta.method: Every term was read from the administrator's own page, the statute, eCFR, IRS, Federal Register (govinfo) or the CHFA QAP on the date in last_checked, and each one carries a verbatim quote and its URL in evidence. A term the official source does not publish is null and listed in unverified with the reason. Nothing is filled from memory or from third-party summaries.
meta.disclaimer: Screening information, not legal or financial advice. Rounds, rates and limits change; confirm every term with the administrator before relying on it.

categories.label: Tax credits
categories.summary: Federal and Colorado credits that bring equity into a deal. The 9% and 4% housing credits are the core of most affordable rental financing in Colorado.

categories.label: CHFA loans
categories.summary: First mortgages, bond loans and gap loans from the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority.

categories.label: Proposition 123 funds
categories.summary: State voter-approved funds for affordable housing. Most require the project to be in a jurisdiction that has filed a Prop 123 commitment.

categories.label: DOLA Division of Housing
categories.summary: State and federal gap funds the Colorado Division of Housing awards through its funding rounds.

categories.label: Federal and private debt, grants and rental assistance
categories.summary: Insured and agency first mortgages, rural programs, Federal Home Loan Bank grants and project-based rental assistance.

categories.label: Local funds
categories.summary: City gap financing. Each city sets its own rounds and terms; other cities and counties run their own programs.

stack.body: Sized to what the restricted rents can carry at a lender's debt coverage ratio. Common sources: CHFA SMART, SIMPLE, CAPABLE and PAIRABLE, FHA 221(d)(4) (up to 90% of cost at 1.11 coverage for affordable projects), Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac affordable loans, and USDA Section 538 guarantees in rural areas.

Usually the largest source. The 9% credit is competitive, awarded by CHFA once a year with a per-project cap. The 4% credit comes with tax-exempt private activity bonds, accepted on a rolling basis; for buildings placed in service in tax years beginning after 2025, bonds need to finance 25% of basis instead of 50%.

The State Affordable Housing Tax Credit is paired with a 9% or 4% award. The Middle-income Housing Tax Credit covers units between 80% and 120% AMI (140% in rural resort counties), which federal credits do not reach.

Fill what debt and equity leave: Prop 123 concessionary debt and equity, Division of Housing grants and loans (HDG, HOME, Housing Trust Fund, CDBG), CHFA gap loans (HOF, CMF), FHLBank Topeka AHP grants and city housing funds. Each adds its own AMI targets, affordability period and, for federal money, environmental review and wage rules.

Units at or below 30% AMI rarely pencil without it. Project-based vouchers from a housing authority and Section 811 rental assistance, plus the Division of Housing supportive housing round, are the main sources.
The last dollar in. CHFA caps the developer fee at 12% to 15% of certain costs, and part of it is often deferred and repaid from cash flow.

considerations.title: AMI elections for tax credit units
considerations.body: A LIHTC project must elect one test: 20% of units at or below 50% AMI, 40% at or below 60% AMI, or the Average Income test (at least 40% of units, designated limits in 10-point steps from 20% to 80% AMI, averaging no more than 60% AMI). The election is irrevocable. Gross rent (including a utility allowance, excluding Section 8 payments) cannot exceed 30% of the unit's imputed income limit. CHFA scoring: for scoring, no more than 60% of low-income units can count at 40% AMI or below unless the project has project-based rental assistance or operating subsidy.

considerations.title: How long units stay affordable
considerations.body: Federal law: 15-year compliance period plus at least 15 more years of extended use. CHFA (adopted 2025-26 QAP and unchanged in the 2027-28 third draft): minimum 15 years of extended use for 4% (with or without state credit) and 25 years for 9% and competitive state credit. The LURA runs at least 30 years. Most state gap sources (Prop 123 and DOH) also require 30 years; see each program below.

considerations.title: Which CHFA allocation plan applies
considerations.body: The adopted plan is the 2025-26 QAP Second Amendment (CHFA Board September 26, 2025; Governor November 13, 2025). The 2027-28 QAP was at its Third Draft (posted September 11, 2026) with Board then Governor approval scheduled for September to October; CHFA's QAP page had not posted an adopted 2027-28 plan as of 2026-10-10. Adopted 2025-26 QAP: $1,800,000 annual 9% credit per project or applicant; $500,000 fixed standard state credit with 9%; Round Two up to $1,300,000 accelerated plus $600,000 standard state credit. 2027-28 third draft (not adopted): 9% cap $1,700,000 (2027) and $1,750,000 (2028), rising to $1,800,000 if state gap funds are unavailable.

considerations.title: Basis boost
considerations.body: Buildings in a HUD Qualified Census Tract or Difficult Development Area get 130% eligible basis. CHFA may designate a 9% building for up to a 30% boost if needed for feasibility, but not if it already qualifies through a QCT, DDA or SADDA, and never for 4% bond deals (federal law bars state-designated boosts for bond-financed buildings). Boosts do not apply to acquisition basis.

considerations.title: Developer fee limits
considerations.body: Developer plus consultant fee: 12% of certain project costs for 51 or more units, 15% for 50 or fewer (new construction and substantial rehab). Up to 5% more for homeless or special-population units at or below 30% AMI, pro-rated by share of units. Builder profit and overhead: 6% to 12% of hard costs depending on size and identity of interest.

considerations.title: 2025 federal tax credit changes
considerations.body: P.L. 119-21 section 70422(a) amends 26 U.S.C. 42(h)(3)(I) to apply a 1.12 multiplier for calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025, with no sunset. P.L. 119-21 section 70422(b) lets a building get 4% credits outside the ceiling if 25% or more of aggregate basis (building plus land) is bond-financed and at least one bond issue dated after December 31, 2025 finances at least 5%; applies to buildings placed in service in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. For 2026 the state housing credit ceiling is the greater of $3.416 per resident or $3,953,600, and the private activity bond volume cap is the greater of $135 per resident or $397,625,000.

considerations.title: Draft 2027-28 plan pairs credits with state gap money
considerations.body: The 2027-28 third draft adds a pilot where 9% and Round Two awardees that request it get a conditional gap award from OEDIT (Prop 123 concessionary debt) or DOH. For 2027 Round One: OEDIT $25 million at $40,000 per unit up to $2.25 million per application; DOH $12 million at $45,000 per unit up to $2.5 million. Draft only. FY2027 AHFF money is reduced: HB26-1360 moved $130M to the General Fund and HB26-1313 advances $80M back, a net $50M cut; about $159M is projected for AHFF programs and $142M for DOLA's Support Fund. Statutory program percentage ranges are waived for FY27 to prioritize tax credit gap funding. The $80M is repaid from FY2028-2029 AHFF allocations.

considerations.title: Prop 123 local commitment
considerations.body: Most Prop 123 money (all OEDIT/CHFA AHFF programs and DOLA homeownership and planning grants) is only available if the project's city, town, county or tribal area has filed a Prop 123 commitment with DOH. A project in an eligible municipality stays eligible even if the county is not. Second-cycle (2027-2029) commitments are due November 1, 2026. A jurisdiction that does not file is ineligible for the following calendar year, which would block projects there in 2027. Fast track: to stay eligible after 2026, each local government must have a review process that reaches a final decision within 90 calendar days of a complete application for developments with 50% or more affordable units, in place by January 1, 2027 (statutory basis C.R.S. 29-32-105(2)). Developers should confirm the jurisdiction's fast-track status. Exemptions: Office of Homeless Initiatives programs and modular/factory-built manufacturer loans do not require a local commitment.

considerations.title: Prop 123 project priorities and closing speed
considerations.body: All AHFF projects must meet three statutory priorities (high density, mixed income meaning three or more income levels, and environmental sustainability including green certification or 2021 IECC, transit proximity, water efficiency, using energy tax credits/rebates and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager reporting); waivers possible with justification. AHFF awards expect quick closings: Land Banking 3-6 months, LIHTC Predevelopment 3-6 months, LIHTC Gap 9 months, Multifamily Finance and Equity 12 months from award notice.

considerations.title: Division of Housing funding rules
considerations.body: DOH-wide rules for its development application: 30-year minimum affordability; at least 5% of rental units at or below 30% AMI; LIHTC income-averaging units up to 80% AMI count if the project averages 60% or below; for-profits get loans (typically 2%); at least 75% of funding confirmed at application; LOI at least 45 days before the deadline. DOH sets maximum incomes and rents in each grant/loan agreement from its published limits; the 2026 HOME rent limits took effect June 1, 2026.

considerations.title: Federal environmental review before you commit
considerations.body: Do not close on land, start demolition or construction, or sign binding contracts before the environmental review clears, even with private money, or the project can lose its HUD funds.

considerations.title: Prevailing wage triggers
considerations.body: Construction contracts covering 12 or more HOME-assisted units must pay Davis-Bacon wages to all laborers and mechanics on the entire project; splitting contracts to avoid this is prohibited. CDBG labor standards apply to nonvolunteer construction labor, but for rehabilitation of residential property only if it has 8 or more units. FHA-insured new construction and substantial rehabilitation must pay Davis-Bacon wages; 223(f) does not.

considerations.title: Section 3 and Buy America
considerations.body: If HUD assistance to the project is over $300,000, the whole project must make efforts to hire low-income workers and Section 3 businesses and report labor hours. Iron, steel, manufactured products and construction materials in federally funded infrastructure projects must be produced in the U.S., subject to HUD's phased implementation schedule and waivers. Small grants waiver: projects with total cost at or below the Simplified Acquisition Threshold of $350,000. De minimis: up to 5% of covered materials cost, maximum $1 million. Project-specific nonavailability waivers require 15-day public comment.

considerations.title: Project-based voucher limits
considerations.body: PHA can project-base up to 20% of authorized vouchers plus 10% for specified populations; per project the greater of 25 units or 25% (40% in difficult-to-use areas), with exceptions. A LIHTC project usually can only get PBVs on about a quarter of its units unless they serve elderly, youth, or supportive-services households.

considerations.title: FHA mortgage insurance premium
considerations.body: All FHA multifamily programs pay 0.25% MIP for applications submitted or amended on or after October 1, 2025; the 2016 Green, Affordable and Broadly Affordable categories are eliminated.

considerations.title: Energy credits are ending
considerations.body: 45L ends for homes acquired after June 30, 2026. 48E excludes wind and solar placed in service after December 31, 2027 unless construction began before July 5, 2026. Pro formas should no longer assume 45L for new units, and new solar on housing that has not begun construction must be in service by end of 2027 to get 48E.

programs.name: Federal 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (CHFA competitive Round One)
programs.administrator: Colorado Housing and Finance Authority (CHFA)
programs.what_it_funds: Equity for new construction, acquisition and rehabilitation of affordable rental housing. Investors buy the 10-year federal credit; CHFA awards it competitively under its Qualified Allocation Plan (QAP).
programs.award_size: Up to $1,800,000 of annual federal 9% credit per project or applicant (adopted 2025-26 QAP). The 2027-28 QAP third draft (not yet adopted) proposes $1,700,000 in 2027 and $1,750,000 in 2028, or $1,800,000 if the state gap-funding pilot money is not available.
programs.rate: 9% applicable percentage floor for new construction and rehabilitation; credit is claimed annually for 10 years.
programs.term: 10-year credit period; 15-year compliance period plus extended use (see affordability_period).
programs.ami_restriction: Owner elects one federal minimum set-aside: 20% of units at or below 50% AMI, 40% at or below 60% AMI, or Average Income (designated limits from 20% to 80% AMI, averaging no more than 60% AMI). CHFA scoring rewards deeper targeting, but no more than 60% of low-income units can count at 40% AMI or below unless the project has rental assistance or operating subsidy.
programs.affordability_period: Adopted 2025-26 QAP: 15-year compliance period plus a minimum 25-year extended-use period for 9% and competitive state credit (40 years total). The LURA runs at least 30 years.
programs.eligible_applicants: An entity that controls the project owner and is not a single purpose entity; consultants cannot be the applicant. At least 10% of the annual federal ceiling is reserved for qualified nonprofit projects (federal law).
programs.eligible_projects: Rental housing that meets QAP threshold criteria; rehabilitation hard costs must exceed the greater of 20% of adjusted basis or $20,000 per unit.
programs.application_cycle: One competitive round per year (Round One, 9% plus standard state credit). The 2026 round closed February 2, 2026. Next: 2027 Round One letter of intent due December 1, 2026 and application due February 1, 2027 by 5:00pm MT, per the 2027-28 QAP third draft, which is not yet adopted.
key_considerations: A letter of intent, a market analyst engagement letter and (if needed) a parking study engagement are due by the LOI deadline, about two months before the application.
A preliminary reservation lasts 13 months; you must spend more than 10% of total project costs to get a carryover allocation, then place in service within two calendar years.
CHFA requires 25 years of extended use for 9% deals, 10 more than the federal minimum, and awards scoring points for the extended-use election.
Developer and consultant fees are capped at 12% (51 or more units) or 15% (50 or fewer units) of certain project costs, and cannot increase after the preliminary award.
A CHFA discretionary basis boost of up to 30% is available only to 9% deals that are not already in a QCT, DDA or SADDA.
The 2027-28 QAP is still a draft (third draft posted September 11, 2026); per-project caps and dates may change before CHFA Board and Governor approval.

programs.name: Federal 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit with tax-exempt Private Activity Bonds (CHFA)
programs.administrator: Colorado Housing and Finance Authority (CHFA); PAB volume cap administered statewide by DOLA Division of Housing
programs.what_it_funds: Non-competitive federal credit equity for rental projects financed with tax-exempt private activity bonds. The credit sits outside the 9% state ceiling but depends on getting bond volume cap.
programs.award_size: No per-project 4% credit cap in the QAP (the $1.8M cap excludes bond deals); credit is sized to need. CHFA's 2026 PAB Fund ($125 million) takes applications for up to $20 million of PAB with a local issuer contribution, or up to $5 million of PAB transferred to a contributing local issuer.
programs.rate: 4% applicable percentage floor (federal minimum for buildings placed in service after December 31, 2020).
programs.ami_restriction: Same federal minimum set-aside elections as 9%: 20/50, 40/60, or Average Income (average no more than 60% AMI).
programs.affordability_period: Adopted 2025-26 QAP: minimum 15-year extended-use period for 4% (with or without state credit) after the 15-year compliance period, so 30 years total; the LURA runs at least 30 years.
programs.eligible_applicants: Same applicant definition as the QAP. The 2026 PAB Fund allows one application per applicant or affiliate.
programs.eligible_projects: Bond-financed new construction or acquisition/rehab. 2026 PAB Fund: new construction, existing projects without credits, existing credit projects in year 20 or later from the start of the credit period, and acquisition/rehab with at least $75,000 per unit of hard cost.
programs.application_cycle: Rolling. Bond-financed 4% applications are accepted all year except February, August and December. 2026 PAB Fund applications are due by 5:00pm MT on the first business day of April, May, July, September, October and November 2026; the last one is the first business day of November 2026. An LOI and concept meeting are required at least 45 days before the application.
key_considerations: You need bond volume cap first. Each year CHFA receives 48% of Colorado's PAB cap and local issuers get the rest; the 2026 CHFA PAB Fund had $87.4 million left as of August 4, 2026.

Federal law now lets a building qualify for 4% credits with bonds financing 25% (down from 50%) of aggregate basis, for buildings placed in service in tax years starting after 2025 if at least 5% is financed by bonds issued after 2025. CHFA's 2026 PAB Fund guidelines still say aggregate basis is limited to the higher of 30% or permanent supportable debt.
CHFA's discretionary 30% basis boost does not apply to 4% deals; only HUD QCT, DDA or SADDA locations get the boost.
CHFA does not offer a 4% PAB Fund waiting list for 2027; reserved bond cap expires 10 business days after the construction loan closing date stated in the application unless extended.
CHFA charges conduit issuer fees (for example 50 basis points upfront on permanent bonds and 20 basis points annually after conversion).

programs.name: Colorado State Affordable Housing Tax Credit (state LIHTC: standard and accelerated)
programs.administrator: Colorado Housing and Finance Authority (CHFA)
programs.what_it_funds: A Colorado income tax credit, claimed over six years and paired with a federal housing tax credit, that adds equity to LIHTC rental projects. Standard credit goes with 9% deals in Round One; accelerated credit goes with 4% bond deals in Round Two.
programs.award_size: Adopted 2025-26 QAP: a fixed $500,000 of standard annual state credit paired with a 9% application; in Round Two up to $1,300,000 of accelerated plus up to $600,000 of standard annual state credit per project or applicant; $10,000 per unit up to $700,000 for 4% bond deals applying in September to November 2025 and 2026. The 2027-28 third draft (not adopted) proposes different fixed amounts (see key considerations).
programs.rate: Six-year credit. Accelerated credit is claimed 70% in year 1 and 6% in years 2 to 6; standard credit is claimed ratably over six years. QAP states the APR for the total six-year state credit allocation is 30% of qualified basis.
programs.term: 6-year credit period
programs.affordability_period: Adopted 2025-26 QAP: competitive state credit requires a 25-year extended-use period after compliance; state credit with 4% requires at least 15 years of extended use. LURA minimum 30 years.
programs.eligible_applicants: Applicants for federal 9% (Round One) or federal 4% bond projects (Round Two and the fall bond window), under the QAP applicant definition.
programs.eligible_projects: Projects that also receive a federal housing tax credit.
programs.application_cycle: Round One (with 9%) and Round Two (with 4%). The 2026 Round Two application closed August 3, 2026. Under the adopted QAP, 4% bond projects may request state credit in September, October and November 2026 as available. Next competitive round: 2027 Round One (LOI December 1, 2026, per the not-yet-adopted 2027-28 draft).
key_considerations: HB24-1434 added accelerated state credit authority of $12 million in 2026 and 2027, $16 million in 2028 and $20 million a year in 2029 to 2031, on top of $10 million a year of standard credit through 2031.
Accelerated credit lets investors claim 70% in year one, which usually raises pricing for 4% deals.
Round Two state credit awards have a milestone: documents are due the first business day of the 18th month after the reservation letter, or the reservation can be revoked.

The 2027-28 third draft proposes, in 2027, a fixed $650,000 of standard credit with 9% and $1.0 million accelerated plus up to $675,000 standard in Round Two; in 2028, $675,000 with 9% and $1.2 million accelerated plus up to $600,000 standard. It also allows Transit Zone credit in place of standard credit where eligible.
Requesting state credit puts the project in CHFA's competitive quiet period from the LOI date to the award announcement.

programs.name: Colorado Middle-income Housing Tax Credit (MIHTC)
programs.administrator: Colorado Housing and Finance Authority (CHFA)
programs.what_it_funds: A stand-alone Colorado tax credit (not paired with federal LIHTC) for rental housing serving households from 80% to 120% AMI, or up to 140% AMI in rural resort counties. Pilot created by HB24-1316.
programs.award_size: No less than $1,650,000 and up to $5,000,000 of MIHTC per project or applicant (2026 amended allocation plan). $5 million of MIHTC is available in 2026; $2,110,000 was shown as available for rolling applications as of September 3, 2026.
programs.rate: Credit is claimed ratably over five years.
programs.term: 5-year credit period
programs.ami_restriction: Middle-income units restricted to households between 80% and 120% AMI, up to 140% AMI in rural resort counties.
programs.affordability_period: At least 15 years and up to 40 years, starting with the first taxable year of the credit period.
programs.eligible_applicants: Applicants under the MIHTC allocation plan; a transferable credit structure is allowed only for governmental or quasi-governmental owners.
programs.eligible_projects: New construction, adaptive reuse, or acquisition and rehabilitation; adaptive reuse and acq/rehab need at least $75,000 of hard cost per unit.
programs.application_cycle: One competitive round (2026 application deadline May 18, 2026), then rolling applications while credit remains: applications due the first business day of August, September, October and November, with the LOI due the first business day of the month before. The only remaining 2026 rolling date is the first business day of November 2026 (LOI was due the first business day of October).
key_considerations: MIHTC is not paired with the federal credit, so it does not carry Section 42 rules; it has its own allocation plan separate from the QAP.
Authorization is $5 million in 2025 and 2026 and $10 million a year in 2027 to 2029, a $40 million pilot total.
Statutory affordability is 15 years minimum; CHFA's plan allows up to 40 years.
Credit is subject to recapture for noncompliance; transferable credits are limited to governmental or quasi-governmental owners.
CHFA's Dates and Deadlines page lists a March 16, 2026 MIHTC LOI date, but the amended plan adopted March 12, 2026 moved it to April 20, 2026. Use the plan.
